item.title: A lint ratchet: from 97 useEffects to 2 in a week
item.description:
Our React frontend had 97 useEffect calls sitting directly in components. Most of them were fine on the day they were written. Together they were the main source of “why did this re-render” and “why is this state one step behind” bugs.

Banning useEffect outright would have failed the build on day one. Leaving it alone meant the count only went up. What worked was a third option: a lint rule that fails on any new effect, plus a list of the existing ones that may only get shorter.

A week later, 2 were left.

The rule

The rule itself is small. It reports useEffect and useLayoutEffect wherever it sees them: called bare, as React.useEffect, through a renamed import, or through a namespace import.

const EFFECT_HOOKS = new Set(["useEffect", "useLayoutEffect"]);

export const noEffectOutsideHooks = {
 meta: { /* ... */ messages: { effectOutsideHook: MESSAGE } },
 create(context) {
 const effectAliases = new Set(EFFECT_HOOKS);
 const namespaces = new Set(["React"]);

 return {
 ImportDeclaration(node) {
 if (node.source.value !== "react") return;
 for (const spec of node.specifiers) {
 if (spec.type === "ImportSpecifier" && EFFECT_HOOKS.has(spec.imported.name)) {
 effectAliases.add(spec.local.name); // import { useEffect as onMount }
 } else if (spec.type !== "ImportSpecifier") {
 namespaces.add(spec.local.name); // import * as R from "react"
 }
 }
 },
 CallExpression(node) {
 if (isEffectCall(node.callee)) {
 context.report({ node: node.callee, messageId: "effectOutsideHook" });
 }
 },
 };
 },
};

The rule doesn’t decide where effects are allowed. That lives in the config: files named use*.ts(x), the UI primitives folder, tests and stories are excluded. So an effect can still exist, but only inside a named custom hook, where its name says what it is for.

The message matters more than the rule. It is the first thing a developer (or an agent) reads when the build fails, so it lists the alternatives in the order you should try them:

Effects live in a named custom hook (a use*.ts(x) file). Before writing one: derive the value during render; reset state with a key; put user-triggered work in the event handler; use React Query hooks for server state, useDebounce for debouncing and useEffectEvent for latest-callback refs.

That is the You Might Not Need an Effect page, compressed into a lint message.

A sister rule does the same for setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame and requestIdleCallback. Timers go through a few approved hooks (useDebounce, useDelayedTrue, a frame scheduler) or they fail lint.

The ratchet

The interesting part is how existing violations are tolerated. A JSON file lists, per file and per rule, how many violations that file may hold:

{
 "src/hooks/useForgeViewer.ts": {
 "app/no-imperative-timers": { "count": 2 }
 }
}

A wrapper around the rule holds back every report until the file is done, then compares the total with the allowed count:

export function ratcheted(ruleId, rule) {
 return {
 meta: { ...rule.meta, messages: { ...rule.meta.messages, staleSuppression: "..." } },
 create(context) {
 const held = [];
 // Hand the inner rule a context whose report() only collects.
 const holding = new Proxy({}, {
 get(_, key) {
 if (key === "report") return (descriptor) => held.push(descriptor);
 const value = context[key];
 return typeof value === "function" ? value.bind(context) : value;
 },
 });
 const { "Program:exit": onExit, ...listeners } = rule.create(holding);
 return {
 ...listeners,
 "Program:exit"(program) {
 onExit?.(program);
 const allowed = allowedCount(context, ruleId);
 if (held.length > allowed) {
 for (const descriptor of held) context.report(descriptor);
 } else if (held.length < allowed) {
 context.report({ node: program, messageId: "staleSuppression", /* ... */ });
 }
 },
 };
 },
 };
}

Three outcomes per file:

  • More than allowed: every violation in the file is reported, so you see all of them and not only the new one.
  • Exactly allowed: silence.
  • Fewer than allowed: lint fails with “run npm run lint:prune-suppressions”. If you remove an effect, you have to lower the count in the same PR. Otherwise the freed slot could be spent again later without anyone noticing.

The empty {} target of the proxy is not decoration. The linter freezes context.report, and a proxy may not return a different value for a frozen property of its own target. Proxying an empty object sidesteps that.

Guarding the guard

A list anyone can edit is a list that grows. Three things stop that.

A test holds a ceiling per file. The JSON file is checked against a hard-coded table in a unit test, with a comment explaining why each remaining entry is still there:

const FILE_CEILINGS = {
 // The 300 ms cap keeps a commit that never settles from freezing the step change.
 "src/hooks/stepViewTransition.ts": { timers: 1 },
 "src/hooks/useCopyToClipboard.ts": { timers: 1 },
 // ...
};

Raising a number means editing both the JSON and this table. That shows up in review as a deliberate change, not as a side effect of rerunning a generator.

The test lints a real file with one extra violation. It takes a file the list still counts, appends one effect, and checks that lint now fails. A second case lints an emptied version of that file and checks that the stale-count message appears. If someone breaks the wrapper, this goes red.

Disable comments can’t switch the rules off. The ratchet would be pointless if // eslint-disable-next-line worked on it. Every disable comment needs a reason on the same line, blanket disables fail, and the two ratchet rules can’t be disabled by comment at all. The list is the only way to tolerate an effect.

Then the cleanup

The rule landed with 97 effects in 61 files. Three hand-rolled 300 ms search debounces were replaced by useDebounce in the same PR, which brought it to 94. Then the cleanup went area by area, one PR per folder or feature, each with a before/after table in the description:

Step Effects in components Timers outside hooks Files on the list
Rule lands 94 in 61 files 39 in 30 files 84
Shell and layout 84 in 53 files 39 76
Shared components 43 in 32 files 36 in 27 files 55
Providers, timer-only hooks 27 in 20 files 32 in 23 files 39
Remaining feature areas 2 32 23

The obvious way to clear the list is to cut each effect out of its component and paste it into a useSomething.ts file. That makes the rule go quiet and changes nothing else. We did some of that, for effects that are real subscriptions: a postMessage bridge, a third-party image cropper, tracking scripts. Each of those hooks has a doc comment saying why it has to be an effect.

But most effects weren’t subscriptions. They were synchronising one piece of state with another, and those could be deleted.

Example: a paginated picker with ten effects

Three CRM picker tables (accounts, contacts, delivery addresses) together held ten effects like these:

useEffect(() => setCurrentPage(1), [debouncedSearchTerm, accountId]);
useEffect(() => setCurrentPage(1), [sorting]);

// Reset selection for a new account or search.
useEffect(() => {
 if (initialSelectedId) setRowSelection({ [initialSelectedId]: true });
 else setRowSelection({});
}, [accountId, initialSelectedId]);

Every one of them renders once with stale state, then again with the reset. With a remote table that can mean a request for page 3 of a search that only has one page.

The replacement is one hook with no effects. Changes the user makes do their resets in the handler:

const setSorting: OnChangeFn<SortingState> = (updater) => {
 setSortingState(updater);
 setCurrentPage(1);
 if (!keepSelectionAcrossPages) setRowSelection({});
};

Changes that arrive from outside an event (a prop, the debounced search term) are compared with the last value seen and adjusted during render. This is React’s documented “adjusting state when a prop changes” pattern:

const [seen, setSeen] = useState({ debouncedSearchTerm, scope, defaultSelectedId });
const searchChanged = seen.debouncedSearchTerm !== debouncedSearchTerm;
const scopeChanged = seen.scope !== scope;

if (searchChanged || scopeChanged) {
 setSeen({ debouncedSearchTerm, scope, defaultSelectedId });
 setCurrentPage(1);
 setRowSelection(selectionOf(defaultSelectedId));
}

React throws away the render that called setState and renders again before anything reaches the screen, so no render ever queries a stale page. Ten effects, three components, one hook, 13 tests.

Other patterns that removed effects

  • A form submitted from a dialog footer used an effect to watch a “submit requested” counter. Now the footer button is a native <button type="submit" form={formId}>. Validation and Enter-to-submit work as before.
  • A tooltip that only opens when text is cut off measured the element in an effect. Now it measures in the pointer-move and focus handlers, right before the tooltip would open, and cancels the event if the text fits. As a side effect it now follows resizes.
  • A “save failed” notice that hides after 6 seconds used an effect plus setTimeout. Now it is a child component keyed on the failure count, using the approved useDelayedTrue hook. Each new failure remounts it, which restarts the timer.
  • A ref that mirrors the latest callback became useEffectEvent.
  • Components that registered refs with a parent in an effect now read from a tiny store with useSyncExternalStore.

One that went back on the list

One PR first moved a 3D viewer’s loading effect into useReportViewerLoading. In review we undid that. The effect copied the viewer’s loading state up into a parent, which is exactly the kind of effect the rule is meant to remove. Hiding it in a hook file only made the rule go quiet. The real fix is to have the parent own that state, and that wasn’t something I could prove safe with the tests we had. So it went back on the list until the follow-up.

That is the rule I’d give anyone doing this: moving an effect into a hook is only progress if the effect is a real subscription. Otherwise you are hiding it from the linter.

What’s left

Two effects and 32 timers. The timers are mostly legitimate: animation fallbacks for an animationend that a reduced-motion setting never sends, a copy-to-clipboard confirmation, a reCAPTCHA poll. Each one has its reason next to its ceiling in the test file, so the next person doesn’t have to work it out again.

Takeaways

  • Ban the pattern, not the code that already uses it. A shrink-only list lets you start enforcing on day one.
  • Make the list hard to grow. A ceiling in a test, no disable comments, and a failure when a count is higher than it needs to be.
  • Put the alternatives in the error message. That is where people (and coding agents) look.
  • Measure progress in the PR description. A before/after table per PR made the cleanup easy to review and kept it moving.

item.title: A robot that clicks around staging every night
item.description:
Our end-to-end tests follow scripts. Open the product, pick an option, go to the summary, check the price. They catch regressions in the paths we wrote down. They don’t catch the crash that only happens when you press Escape in a dialog, go Back, and click something else.

So we added a test that doesn’t follow a script. Every night it opens our React product configurator on staging and clicks around at random for a few minutes, checking every screen it lands on. When it finds something, it prints a command that replays the exact same walk.

On its second night it found a memory leak in our 3D viewer.

What a walk does

Each walk starts from an entry page (home, the product list, the configurator) and repeats:

  1. Pick an action, weighted: click, type or select on a visible control (80%), Tab (7%), Escape (7%), Shift+Tab (3%), browser Back (3%).
  2. Wait for the app to settle.
  3. Check the screen.
const ACTIONS = [
 { value: "control", weight: 80 },
 { value: "tab", weight: 7 },
 { value: "shift-tab", weight: 3 },
 { value: "escape", weight: 7 },
 { value: "back", weight: 3 },
];

When it types into a field, it picks from a small list of inputs that hand-written tests rarely try:

export const FILL_CORPUS = [
 "", "a", "x".repeat(300), "Ünïcødé ✓ 日本語 🚀", "<b>bold</b>",
 "42", "-1", "0", "1e9", "3.14",
];

After every step, it checks:

  • no uncaught error and no console.error
  • no API response with status 500 or higher
  • no raw translation key on screen (summary.dialog.title instead of a label)
  • no undefined, NaN or [object Object] on screen
  • the page isn’t blank, has exactly one <main> and at most one visible <h1>
  • focus doesn’t drop to <body> after Escape

Five walks run in a GitHub Actions workflow at 03:30, after the normal scripted suite. It never runs on pull requests and isn’t a required check. Its job is to find things, not to block merges.

Same seed, same walk

A random test is only useful if you can reproduce what it found. All randomness comes from one seeded generator. It is mulberry32, inline, because the walk needs nothing more than a 32-bit stream that replays the same way on every machine:

export function mulberry32(seed: number): Random {
 let state = seed >>> 0;
 return () => {
 state = (state + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
 let t = state;
 t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1);
 t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61);
 return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
 };
}

Each run has one base seed (the CI run id, or Date.now() locally). Each walk mixes in its own name with FNV-1a, so the five walks differ from each other but any one can be replayed on its own:

export function walkSeed(base: string | number, walk: string): number {
 let hash = 0x811c9dc5;
 for (const char of `${base}:${walk}`) {
 hash ^= char.codePointAt(0) ?? 0;
 hash = Math.imul(hash, 0x01000193) >>> 0;
 }
 return hash >>> 0;
}

A failure names the rule, the step, the URL and the seed, and the job summary gets a command like this:

E2E_EXPLORE=1 E2E_SEED=20261116 E2E_STEPS=16 \
 npx playwright test --project=explore-chromium --grep "walk from home"

E2E_STEPS stops the replay at the failing step, so you land on the broken screen in Playwright’s UI mode instead of watching 400 steps go by.

One limit is worth stating: the seed fixes which actions the walk chooses. It doesn’t fix what a shared staging backend returns or how long it takes. In practice the replay hits the same bug almost every time, but not always.

It must not break staging

Staging is shared with the whole team. A robot that clicks every button would eventually request quotes, upload files and edit customer records. Steering it away from dangerous buttons isn’t enough, because buttons get renamed. So safety has two layers.

Steering. The walk never touches file inputs, type=submit buttons, download links, links that open a new tab, links that leave the app, or a short list of names like the “send request” button (in all nine languages, because the walk can switch language).

The guarantee is at the network layer. Every request goes through page.route, and every write to the API is aborted unless it is on an allow-list:

export function blockReason(method: string, rawUrl: string): string | null {
 if (READ_METHODS.has(method.toUpperCase())) return null;
 const url = new URL(rawUrl);
 if (!isOurApi(url.hostname)) return null;

 const blocked = BLOCKED_WRITES.find(({ pattern }) => pattern.test(url.pathname));
 if (blocked) return blocked.reason;
 const allowed = ALLOWED_WRITES.some(
 ({ methods, pattern }) => methods.has(method) && pattern.test(url.pathname)
 );
 if (allowed) return null;
 return "write to an endpoint the walk does not allow";
}

The allow-list is the draft-configuration endpoints, verb by verb, with real GUIDs for ids (so a path like /configurator/pdf can’t pass as an id). Each entry also names its HTTP methods, so a stray DELETE to a draft path is blocked too. Anything with quot in the path is always blocked.

The important part is the last line. A new endpoint that writes data is blocked by default and shows up as a blocked-request violation. It fails closed. That is the opposite of what my first draft did, which was a list of endpoints to block.

The walk also stubs window.print and window.open, and dismisses any stray browser dialog.

Settling without a destination

The usual Playwright advice is to wait for a specific element, never a fixed time. A random walk has no destination to wait for. And networkidle doesn’t help in a single-page app: it resolves at once.

So the walk tracks requests itself and waits until none have been in flight for 400 ms, capped at 5 seconds so a streaming 3D model can’t stall it:

export function trackRequests(page: Page) {
 const inFlight = new Set<Request>();
 let lastChange = Date.now();
 const touch = () => (lastChange = Date.now());
 page.on("request", (r) => inFlight.add(r) && touch());
 page.on("requestfinished", (r) => inFlight.delete(r) && touch());
 page.on("requestfailed", (r) => inFlight.delete(r) && touch());

 return {
 async settle() {
 const until = Date.now() + 5000;
 await pause(100); // let a request the last action triggered register
 while (Date.now() < until) {
 if (!inFlight.size && Date.now() - lastChange >= 400) return;
 await pause(100);
 }
 },
 };
}

A screen that fails a check is read again 1.5 seconds later, and only violations that are still there count. Without that, every loading skeleton caught mid-transition would be a failure.

Keeping the rules honest

Rules live outside the browser. Everything that decides is a pure function with unit tests: the PRNG, the action filter, the network block, the screen rules, the allow-list matcher. The Playwright side only reads facts from the page and drives the walk. That makes the rules cheap to test and keeps flakes out of them.

A walk that does nothing fails. A walk of 10 or more steps that never clicked, filled or selected a control fails as no-control-acted, instead of passing green because it spent five minutes pressing Tab on an error page.

I checked that each rule can fail. Before merging I put one violation of each kind into a real walk: an uncaught error, a console.error, a 500, a blocked write, a raw key, NaN, two <h1>s, a blank page, lost focus. All nine went red with the rule, step, URL, seed and replay command.

Known bugs go on a narrow list. Two things on main already failed the walk on day one. They went into a KNOWN_VIOLATIONS list, each matched on its rule plus a narrow regex, with a reason. Entries only ever get removed:

const DIALOG_OUTLIVES_ROUTE: KnownViolation = {
 rule: "focus-lost",
 // Only a dialog that outlived its route: opened on one path, now on another.
 detail: /\(dialog opened on (\S+), now on (?!\1\))\S+\)$/,
 reason:
 "dialog state sits above the routes, so a dialog stays open after browser Back; " +
 "closing it then has no trigger to return focus to",
};

The regex is the point. A dialog that loses focus on its own route still fails.

What it found

A WebGL viewer that never died

Two nights in, a walk failed at step 484 with:

console-error: Rendering to a canvas that was resized to zero. If you see this message
you may be accidentally leaking a viewer instance. ErrorCode:14.

It was followed by dozens of Cannot set properties of null (setting 'shareDepthFrom').

Our 3D view wraps Autodesk’s viewer. Leaving a 3D step while the viewer was still waiting for its auth token went like this:

  1. React unmounted the component, and our hook removed the element.
  2. The token arrived.
  3. The wrapper built Autodesk’s Viewer3D on the detached, zero-sized element and started its render loop. Nothing ever stopped it.

Even without the error burst, every visit to a 3D step left one live viewer and one WebGL context behind. window.NOP_VIEWERS.length went up by one per visit.

A colleague added an idempotent dispose() to the wrapper package, and the hook now calls it on every path that drops a viewer: unmount, both cancelled-init paths and the failed-init catch. Each of the four cases has a test that fails on the old hook.

No scripted test would have found this. You have to leave the page during a window of a few hundred milliseconds, on a slow network, and then keep going for a while.

A focus check that raced the UI library

The walk also failed with “Escape dropped focus” on an image preview dialog. The failure snapshot showed focus on the opener, so the app was right and the check was wrong.

Radix returns focus in a setTimeout(0) after the dialog unmounts, so between unmount and that timeout document.activeElement is <body>. On a fast machine that gap is 5 ms. With 20x CPU throttling it’s 116 ms. The CI runner, busy rendering 3D, read focus right in that window.

The fix wasn’t to drop the rule. The check now reads focus every 50 ms and only reports a loss if focus is still on <body> after 1.5 seconds. If focus is already on an element it reads once and doesn’t wait.

Smaller things

  • A product on staging returned a 500 without CORS headers, so the browser could only report it as a CORS error.
  • A link in the header with no accessible name.
  • A dialog that stays open after browser Back (the known violation above).

Takeaways

  • Seed everything and print the replay command. A random test without a replay is a flaky test.
  • Make safety fail closed. Allow-list writes at the network layer, and treat a blocked write as a finding.
  • Keep the decisions in pure functions. The browser side should only read and act.
  • Check every rule can fail before trusting it green.
  • Expect to fix your own checks. One of the first three failures was the test being wrong about timing. That’s fine, as long as the fix keeps the rule strict.

item.title: Property-based tests found two bugs our example tests never would
item.description:
Example tests check the cases you thought of. Property-based tests check a rule against inputs you didn’t think of. I’d known that for years and never got round to adding them to our React frontend.

When we did, using fast-check, two of the first eight property files found real bugs. Neither was exotic. Both were the kind of in and ?? code most JavaScript codebases have.

Bug 1: a saved cart where “abc” counts as 3

The app keeps a quote cart in localStorage: a JSON list of configuration ids and a JSON map of quantities. Reading it looked like this:

this.savedIds = this.parseOr<string[]>(raw, []);

parseOr returns the fallback when JSON.parse throws. That covers garbage. It doesn’t cover valid JSON in the wrong shape, which is what you get from an older version of the app on the same origin, another tab, or someone editing values in DevTools:

Stored value Result
null crash: null.includes is not a function
"abc" a cart with 3 items: "a", "b", "c"
{"a":1} crash further down

The type annotation <string[]> made it look checked. It wasn’t.

The fix validates the shape and keeps only what a cart can hold:

function toConfigurationIds(value: unknown): string[] {
 if (!Array.isArray(value)) return [];
 return [...new Set(value.filter((id): id is string => typeof id === "string" && id !== ""))];
}

function toQuantities(value: unknown): Record<string, number> {
 if (value === null || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) return {};
 return Object.fromEntries(
 Object.entries(value).filter(([, n]) => Number.isInteger(n) && (n as number) >= 1)
 );
}

There was a second bug in the same code. The quantity lookup was stored[id] ?? 1. For an id named toString, stored[id] isn’t undefined. It’s Object.prototype.toString, a function, so the summary page showed a function as the quantity. Every reader of a cart quantity now goes through one helper that checks own keys:

export const cartQuantity = (stored: Record<string, number>, id: string) =>
 Object.hasOwn(stored, id) ? stored[id] : 1;

Bug 2: a translation named valueOf crashes the app

Admins can override the app’s built-in labels. The merge only applies an override if the key exists in the bundled messages and the override keeps the same ICU placeholders:

for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(remoteMessages)) {
 if (!(key in bundledMessages)) continue;
 // ...validate placeholders against the default, then apply
}

key in bundledMessages is true for "valueOf", because in walks the prototype chain. The validation then took defaultMessages["valueOf"] (a function), called .matchAll on it, and threw. One oddly named key from the admin side would have broken every label in the app.

fast-check shrank the failure to this:

Counterexample: [{}, {"valueOf":"'"}, {}]

Empty bundle, one remote key named valueOf, empty defaults. You can see the bug from the counterexample alone.

The fix is two Object.hasOwn calls. The counterexample stays in the suite as a normal example test.

How the properties are written

The properties are mostly simple statements:

const RUNS = { seed: 4075, numRuns: 100 };

it("never throws, never adds a key and takes each value from the bundle or the remote", () => {
 fc.assert(
 fc.property(messages, messages, messages, (bundled, remote, defaults) => {
 const merged = mergeRemoteMessages(bundled, remote, defaults);
 expect(Object.keys(merged)).toEqual(Object.keys(bundled));
 for (const k of Object.keys(merged)) {
 expect([bundled[k], remote[k]]).toContain(merged[k]);
 }
 }),
 RUNS
 );
});

it("is idempotent", () => {
 fc.assert(
 fc.property(messages, messages, messages, (bundled, remote, defaults) => {
 const once = mergeRemoteMessages(bundled, remote, defaults);
 expect(mergeRemoteMessages(once, remote, defaults)).toEqual(once);
 }),
 RUNS
 );
});

Two choices made the difference between properties that find things and properties that only pass.

Build generators from the input’s own tokens. A random string almost never contains valid ICU syntax, so a property fed fc.string() only ever tests the “reject garbage” branch. Building messages from ICU pieces reaches the interesting code:

const icuMessage = fc
 .array(
 fc.constantFrom(
 "{", "}", "'", "#", " ", "Label", "{count}", "{name}",
 "{count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}",
 "<b>", "</b>", "<link>go</link>", "l'<b>"
 ),
 { maxLength: 8 }
 )
 .map((tokens) => tokens.join(""));

Put the dangerous values in the generator on purpose. The key generator is a short list that includes toString, constructor and valueOf. fast-check would rarely produce those names from random strings. Once they’re in the list, it hits them within a few runs.

const key = fc.constantFrom("a", "b", "c", "d", "toString", "constructor", "valueOf");

Pin the seed. Every fc.assert gets a fixed seed and numRuns. CI is deterministic, and a failure prints the seed and path needed to replay it.

A model test for the cart

A cart has more behaviour than a single function: add, duplicate, change a quantity, remove, submit a quote, reload. Bugs tend to be in the order of operations. fast-check’s model-based testing generates sequences of commands, runs them against the real code and against a simple model, and checks they agree after every step.

The model is just what a visitor would say is in the cart:

interface CartModel {
 ids: string[];
 quantities: Record<string, number>;
 current: string | null;
 multiple: boolean | undefined; // the "multiple configurations" setting
}

Each command updates the model, calls the real service, then checks every cart rule against what the service reads back:

const commit = configurationId.map((id) =>
 command(`Commit(${id})`, async (model) => {
 await cartService.commitConfiguration(id, { enableMultipleConfigurations: model.multiple });
 if (model.multiple === false) {
 model.ids = [id];
 model.quantities = {};
 } else if (!model.ids.includes(id)) {
 model.ids = [...model.ids, id];
 }
 model.current = id;
 })
);

There are seven commands: Commit, Duplicate, SetQuantity, Remove, SubmitQuote, Reload, and ForeignWrite. The last one is the important one. It writes something into localStorage behind the app’s back (valid JSON, unparseable text, prototype names, empty strings, duplicates) and works out on its own what the cart should read as. That is how the wrong-shape bug turned into a permanent regression test rather than a one-off fix.

The test runs 2000 sequences of up to 30 steps against the real storage service and takes about 0.25 seconds.

Do the tests actually catch anything?

A property that can’t fail is worse than no test, because it looks like coverage. So before merging, the reviewer and I made deliberate mutations to the source (flip a comparison, drop a filter, swap an Object.hasOwn back to in) and checked which ones turned a test red. 29 of 33 mutations did. The four that didn’t are listed in the PR, with a note on why: mostly mutations that don’t change behaviour for any input the app can produce.

A free speed-up

One property checked that sorting search results by name is stable and drops nothing. While writing it I noticed the comparator stripped HTML from both names with DOMParser on every comparison. That’s O(n log n) DOM parses for a sort. Stripping each key once before sorting made those properties run 3 to 6 times faster, with the same order.

Takeaways

  • in and ?? on objects keyed by user data are bugs waiting for a key named toString. Use Object.hasOwn, or a Map.
  • A TypeScript annotation on JSON.parse is a promise, not a check. Validate the shape at the boundary.
  • Generators decide what you test. Build them from real tokens and add the edge cases by hand.
  • Keep the shrunk counterexample as an example test. It documents the bug better than any description.
  • Mutate the code to check the tests. It’s the fastest way to find a property that passes regardless.

item.title: Replacing ESLint with Oxlint, custom rules included
item.description:
Our React frontend ran oxlint && eslint on every pull request. Oxlint finished in 0.6 seconds. ESLint took 16.7. We kept ESLint for two reasons: a handful of plugins, and our own lint rules (see the lint ratchet post).

Oxlint now supports JavaScript plugins written against the ESLint rule API. So we tried running everything on Oxlint, and ended up removing ESLint completely.

The short version:

Measurement (Apple M5, median of 5 runs) Before After
npm run lint 16.99 s 2.07 s
Lint steps in a PR (fmt:check + lint) 17.44 s 3.24 s
Pre-commit hook, one staged file 2.74 s 3.53 s (slower)

The rest of this post is about the parts the table doesn’t show.

One toolchain: Vite+

We moved to Vite+ at the same time. It bundles Vite, Vitest, Oxlint and the Oxfmt formatter as one dependency, pinned together, with one CLI: vp dev, vp build, vp test, vp lint, vp fmt.

vp migrate did most of the mechanical work. The diff touched 526 files, but almost all of it was one line per file: from "vitest" became from "vite-plus/test".

The lint config moves into vite.config.ts:

import { defineConfig } from "vite-plus";
import { lintConfig } from "./config/lint.config.ts";

export default defineConfig({
 lint: lintConfig,
 staged: {
 "*": "vp fmt",
 "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}": "vp lint --fix",
 },
 // ...
});

The staged block replaced lint-staged. Husky stayed for the git hooks.

What left package.json: eslint, typescript-eslint, @eslint/js, globals, and the react-hooks, react-refresh, import-x, eslint-comments and storybook plugins. About 80 packages left node_modules.

Custom rules as an Oxlint JS plugin

Our own rules were already written against the ESLint rule API (meta, create(context), AST visitors). They load into Oxlint unchanged as a plugin:

// scripts/lint-rules/plugin.mjs
export default {
 meta: { name: "app" },
 rules: {
 "no-effect-outside-hooks": ratcheted("app/no-effect-outside-hooks", noEffectOutsideHooks),
 "no-imperative-timers": ratcheted("app/no-imperative-timers", noImperativeTimers),
 "no-restricted-dynamic-imports": noRestrictedDynamicImports,
 "no-manual-memoization": noManualMemoization,
 "require-disable-description": requireDisableDescription,
 // ...eight rules about disable comments in total
 },
};

// config/lint.config.ts
export const lintConfig = {
 jsPlugins: ["./scripts/lint-rules/plugin.mjs"],
 rules: { "app/no-effect-outside-hooks": "error", /* ... */ },
};

Two things had to be rebuilt rather than ported.

Bulk suppressions. ESLint 9 can store existing violations in a suppressions file. Oxlint can’t. Our ratchet rules now read the file themselves: a wrapper holds back a rule’s reports until the end of the file and compares the count with the file’s entry.

The eslint-comments plugin. We used it to require a reason on every disable comment and to forbid disabling certain rules. It peer-depends on ESLint, so it had to go. Eight small rules in our own plugin replace it. They still read // eslint-disable-next-line rule -- reason comments, because Oxlint honours that spelling.

Testing lint rules without lintText

ESLint has a Node API: give it a string and a file path, get back messages. We used that to test the config itself, for example “a file in src/api may not import from src/components”.

Oxlint has no such API. The replacement writes the code to a temp folder at the same relative path as the real file, next to a copy of the real config, and runs the binary:

export async function lintText(code: string, filePath: string): Promise<LintMessage[]> {
 const dir = await mkdtemp(path.join(tmpdir(), "lint-probe-"));
 try {
 const file = path.join(dir, filePath);
 await mkdir(path.dirname(file), { recursive: true });
 await writeFile(file, code);
 await writeFile(path.join(dir, ".oxlintrc.json"), probeConfig);
 // Oxlint exits non-zero when it reports an error, which is what most probes want.
 const { stdout } = await run(OXLINT, ["-c", ".oxlintrc.json", "-f", "json", filePath], {
 cwd: dir,
 }).catch((failure) => ({ stdout: failure.stdout ?? "" }));
 return JSON.parse(stdout).diagnostics.map(toLintMessage);
 } finally {
 await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
 }
}

Override globs in the config are relative to the config file, so a probe at src/api/x.ts in the temp folder gets exactly the rules the real src/api/x.ts would. The only change to the config is making the plugin path absolute.

It’s slower than an in-process API, about a process spawn per probe. For a few hundred config tests that is fine.

What broke quietly

These are the ones worth knowing before you try this.

Import-ban patterns match differently. ESLint’s no-restricted-imports matches a group pattern gitignore-style. Oxlint matches it as a glob. So @/services/* stopped matching @/services/a/b, and lint stayed green. We only noticed because the boundary tests probe a nested import. The fix is to spell every level out:

// Matches the folder itself and everything beneath it, in both matchers.
const under = (...dirs: string[]) => dirs.flatMap((dir) => [`@/${dir}`, `@/${dir}/**`]);

If you have layer rules and no tests for them, check this by hand.

A rule name with a plugin prefix still disables the built-in rule. In Oxlint, // eslint-disable-next-line x/no-restricted-imports disables the built-in no-restricted-imports. Our “you may not disable this rule” check compared full names, so it needed to compare the bare rule name.

A blanket disable silences its own report. /* eslint-disable */ also turns off the rule that is supposed to complain about blanket disables. That guard is now a test that scans every linted file for one.

A peer dependency on the old Vite+ range. Storybook declared an optional peer of vite-plus ^0.1 || ^0.2, which made npm install fail against 1.7. An overrides entry fixes it.

New findings. Oxlint’s port of the React Compiler purity rule flags new Date().getFullYear() in a footer. ESLint’s didn’t. And react/only-export-components reports 14 warnings the old plugin didn’t.

What we lost

  • All 11 eslint-plugin-storybook rules. There is no Oxlint equivalent and the plugin needs ESLint. Nothing checks our stories now. This is the biggest loss, and the plan is to write the few rules we care about into our own plugin.
  • import-x/order. It was only a warning. Oxfmt’s sortImports can replace it, but turning it on reorders imports across the whole repo once.
  • Editor feedback for two guards. The per-file ceiling and the blanket-disable scan are Vitest tests now. CI still enforces them, but the editor and the commit hook don’t show them.
  • The editor, partly. The Oxlint language server does run JS plugin rules while you type, but only when it finds a .oxlintrc.json. With the config inside vite.config.ts it showed nothing in my test. I haven’t tried the Vite+ editor extension yet.

What got slower

The pre-commit hook went from 2.74 s to 3.53 s. Formatting the repo with vp fmt is 0.46 s slower than calling oxfmt directly, and vp staged is 0.28 s slower than lint-staged. That’s the price of going through one CLI. It runs once per commit, so we accepted it, but the “everything gets faster” story isn’t true for every step.

The risk

The Oxlint docs still call JS plugins alpha. Every custom rule we have now depends on that API. What makes that acceptable for us:

  • vite-plus is pinned to an exact version, so an Oxlint upgrade is always its own PR.
  • The config tests lint real probes through the real binary. If a plugin API change breaks a rule, the upgrade PR goes red.
  • The rules are written against the ESLint rule API. If the alpha stalls, ESLint can host them again.

Was it worth it?

For us, yes. Lint dropped from 17 seconds to 2, we have one dependency where there were six, and none of our own guardrails were lost. But “Oxlint is a drop-in replacement” undersells the work. Test your import bans, list the plugins you’d lose, and time the commit hook as well as the full lint.

item.title: Six months of agentic coding: what actually changed
item.description:
Since May I’ve led a team where coding agents do most of the typing. In that time I merged a little under 500 pull requests across our platform, our 3D viewer and the conversion tooling behind it.

The number says less than it seems to. Typing was never the bottleneck. What changed is where my attention goes, and this post is about that.

1. I write constraints, not code

Most of my corrections to an agent are not about logic. They are about things the codebase can’t tell it:

  • “We use oxfmt here, not prettier.”
  • “Don’t use public packages for this, we maintain a fork.”
  • “Treat the node tree as an API contract.”

Each of those cost me a wasted run the first time. Now they live in the repository, in an AGENTS.md or in memory the agent reads at the start of a session. A correction I have to give twice is a missing line in that file.

2. The builder should not grade its own work

An agent that implements a feature and then reviews it will tell you it looks good. The fix is the same as with people: separate the roles.

We run a builder and a separate critic that has not seen the builder’s reasoning, only the result and the bar it has to meet. For UI work the bar is the design, and the critic compares screenshots against it. The loop repeats until the critic can’t tell which is which, or until it is clear the approach is wrong.

Context separation is the part that matters. When I let both roles share one context, the critic inherited the builder’s blind spots.

3. Small pull requests matter more, not less

An agent will happily produce a 4,000-line pull request. Nobody can review that, and an AI reviewer can’t either.

What works for us:

  • Stacked pull requests. One concern each, reviewed in order.
  • An automated reviewer on every pull request, with written “lenses” for the things we care about, such as the data types in a database migration.
  • One round of rework on the reviewer’s remarks, then a human decides.

4. Verify like a user

“Tests pass” is the weakest claim an agent can make. For anything visual I ask for proof from the running application: open the page, click through the flow, take the screenshot.

It is slower. It also catches the things that would otherwise reach a customer, like a 3D scene that renders on desktop and is black on a phone.

5. Hygiene pays twice

Linting, formatting, audit gates, test coverage and release automation used to be things a team got around to. With agents they are cheap to add, and they pay back immediately, because every guard in CI is a mistake an agent can’t merge.

What didn’t change

  • Someone still has to know what good looks like.
  • Someone still has to talk to the customer.
  • Someone is still accountable for what ships.

The work moved from writing code to deciding what should exist and checking that it does. I find I like that part of the job more.

item.title: Why std::expected matters for error handling
item.description:
C++23 introduced std::expected, changing how we handle errors without exceptions. When you combine it with std::error_code (available since C++11), you get an error handling approach that forces explicit error checks while keeping your code readable. For the C++17 pieces used below, such as std::optional and std::variant, see Practical C++17 highlights by example.

The real power comes from std::error_code carrying more than just a number. Through std::error_category, it associates error codes with human-readable messages and std::error_condition values, letting you classify errors by severity (fatal, warning, informational) rather than checking individual error codes.

When to use std::expected

std::expected<T, E> shines when you need clear separation between success and failure:

  • Type safety: The return value and error are distinct types. You can’t accidentally use an error as a valid result.
  • Explicit checks: You must check for errors before accessing the value. No more forgetting to check return codes.
  • Functional composition: Chain operations cleanly with transform() and or_else(): 
    return readFile(path)
 .transform([](auto content) { return parse(content); })
 .or_else([](auto error) { return handleError(error); });

When to combine it with std::error_code

std::error_code makes sense for non-throwing APIs where you need more context than a simple integer:

  • No exceptions: Perfect for performance-critical code, embedded systems, or codebases with -fno-exceptions.
  • Rich error context: Unlike int VALUE_NOT_FOUND = 100, error codes come with categories and conditions. You can check if an error is “file-related” without knowing every possible file error code.
  • Cross-library consistency: Standard categories like std::generic_category() and std::system_category() work across different libraries.

The combination std::expected<T, std::error_code> gives you the best of both worlds—type-safe error handling with rich error information.

Why choose std::expected over std::error_code alone?

This is a common question, and the answer reveals the design philosophy behind C++ error handling.

std::error_code represents an error value, which typically is an integer code plus an error category. It’s powerful but requires discipline: you can accidentally ignore it, and the error is separate from your return value (often using output parameters or special sentinel values).

std::expected<T, E> takes a different approach. It’s a type-safe container that holds either a value or an error, never both, never neither. The compiler forces you to check which one you have before accessing the value. Think of it like Rust’s Result<T, E> or Haskell’s Either.

Here’s what sets them apart:

Aspect std::error_code std::expected<T, E>
Type safety Error separate from value; manual checks Value and error bundled; compiler-enforced checks
Return style Output parameters or sentinel values Direct return type
Error propagation Manual: if (ec) return ec; Functional: .transform(), .or_else()
Forgetting to check Possible—compiler won’t warn Impossible—can’t access value without checking
Performance Very cheap (integer + pointer) Also cheap (no allocations, just a tagged union)
Best for Legacy APIs, system integration Modern APIs, composable code

The best pattern? Use them together: std::expected<T, std::error_code>. You get type-safe control flow from std::expected plus standardized error reporting from std::error_code.

Practical examples

Traditional approach with std::error_code

Here’s the classic pattern—error code as return value, actual data as output parameter:

#include <fstream>
#include <filesystem>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>

std::string read_file(const std::filesystem::path& path, std::error_code& ec) {
 std::ifstream file(path, std::ios::binary);
 if (!file.is_open()) {
 ec = std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory);
 return {};
 }

 std::string content;
 file.seekg(0, std::ios::end);
 content.resize(file.tellg());
 file.seekg(0, std::ios::beg);

 if (!file.read(content.data(), content.size())) {
 ec = std::make_error_code(std::errc::io_error);
 return {};
 }

 ec.clear();
 return content;
}

int main() {
 std::error_code ec;
 std::string contents = read_file("foo.txt", ec);

 if (ec) {
 std::cerr << "Error: " << ec.message() << "\n";
 return 1;
 }
 // use contents...
}

This works, but notice:

  • The function signature doesn’t clearly show what it returns
  • You could forget to check ec and use contents anyway
  • Output parameters make the API less composable

Modern approach with std::expected

The same functionality with std::expected is clearer:

#include <expected>
#include <fstream>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>
#include <filesystem>
#include <iostream>

std::expected<std::string, std::error_code>
read_file(const std::filesystem::path& path) {
 std::ifstream file(path, std::ios::binary);
 if (!file.is_open()) {
 return std::unexpected(
 std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory));
 }

 std::string content;
 file.seekg(0, std::ios::end);
 content.resize(file.tellg());
 file.seekg(0, std::ios::beg);

 if (!file.read(content.data(), content.size())) {
 return std::unexpected(std::make_error_code(std::errc::io_error));
 }

 return content;
}

int main() {
 auto result = read_file("foo.txt");
 if (!result) {
 std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().message() << "\n";
 return 1;
 }

 std::cout << result.value();
}

Creating custom error categories with HTTP status codes

std::error_code becomes powerful when you define domain-specific categories. HTTP response codes are a perfect example—everyone knows what 404 or 500 means, but you still want to classify them generically (client error vs server error).

Here’s a real implementation for HTTP status codes:

// @file http_response_code.h
#pragma once

#include <system_error>
#include <type_traits>

namespace network {
 enum class http_response_code {
 OK = 200,
 CREATED = 201,
 NO_CONTENT = 204,
 BAD_REQUEST = 400,
 UNAUTHORIZED = 401,
 FORBIDDEN = 403,
 NOT_FOUND = 404,
 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR = 500,
 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE = 503,
 // ... (complete list in actual code)
 };

 enum class http_error_condition {
 INFORMATIONAL = 100,
 SUCCESS = 200,
 REDIRECT = 300,
 CLIENT_ERROR = 400,
 SERVER_ERROR = 500,
 };

 const std::error_category& http_error_category() noexcept;

 // Found through argument-dependent lookup, so they must live in the enums' namespace
 inline std::error_code make_error_code(http_response_code code) noexcept {
 return {static_cast<int>(code), http_error_category()};
 }

 inline std::error_condition make_error_condition(http_error_condition cond) noexcept {
 return {static_cast<int>(cond), http_error_category()};
 }
}

// Register with the type system
namespace std {
 template <>
 struct is_error_code_enum<network::http_response_code> : std::true_type {};

 template <>
 struct is_error_condition_enum<network::http_error_condition> : std::true_type {};
}

// @file http_response_code.cpp
#include "http_response_code.h"

#include <string>

namespace network {
 class http_error_category_impl final : public std::error_category {
 public:
 [[nodiscard]] const char* name() const noexcept override {
 return "http";
 }

 // Error codes close to messages.
 [[nodiscard]] std::string message(int ev) const override {
 switch (static_cast<http_response_code>(ev)) {
 case http_response_code::OK: return "OK";
 case http_response_code::NOT_FOUND: return "Not Found";
 case http_response_code::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR: return "Internal Server Error";
 // ...
 default: return "(unrecognized error)";
 }
 }

 // std::error_condition classification
 std::error_condition default_error_condition(int ev) const noexcept override {
 const auto code = static_cast<http_response_code>(ev);
 if (code >= http_response_code::OK && code < http_response_code(300))
 return make_error_condition(http_error_condition::SUCCESS);
 if (code >= http_response_code(400) && code < http_response_code(500))
 return make_error_condition(http_error_condition::CLIENT_ERROR);
 if (code >= http_response_code(500))
 return make_error_condition(http_error_condition::SERVER_ERROR);

 return std::error_condition(ev, *this);
 }

 bool equivalent(const std::error_code& code, int condition) const noexcept override {
 return *this == code.category() &&
 static_cast<int>(default_error_condition(code.value()).value()) == condition;
 }

 bool equivalent(int code, const std::error_condition& condition) const noexcept override {
 return default_error_condition(code) == condition;
 }
 };

 const std::error_category& http_error_category() noexcept {
 static http_error_category_impl instance;
 return instance;
 }
}

Now you can use it elegantly:

using namespace network;

class http_response {
public:
 std::error_code code{};
 std::string body{};

 [[nodiscard]] bool success() const noexcept {
 return code == make_error_condition(http_error_condition::SUCCESS);
 }
};

// Usage
auto response = http_client.get("https://api.example.com/users");

// Check specific code
if (response.code == http_response_code::NOT_FOUND) {
 std::cerr << "Resource not found\n";
}

// Or check generic condition - this is the power of error_condition
if (response.code == http_error_condition::CLIENT_ERROR) {
 // Handles 400, 401, 403, 404, etc. without checking each one
 std::cerr << "Client error: " << response.code.message() << "\n";
}

if (response.code == http_error_condition::SERVER_ERROR) {
 // Handles 500, 503, etc.
 retry_request();
}

The beauty here: you can check for broad categories (CLIENT_ERROR) without knowing every specific code. This is what makes std::error_condition valuable—it carries the semantic weight of error classification.

Chaining operations functionally

One of the biggest advantages of std::expected is composability. You can chain operations without nested if-statements. Here’s a real-world example from XML parsing:

// Get a child element by name
std::expected<XmlElement*, std::error_code>
get_child_element(XmlElement* parent, std::string_view name) {
 auto child = parent->first_child_element(name.data());
 if (!child)
 return std::unexpected(xml_errc::node_not_found);
 return child;
}

// Extract text from an element
std::expected<std::string, std::error_code>
get_element_text(const XmlElement* element) {
 const char* text = element->get_text();
 if (!text)
 return std::unexpected(xml_errc::node_empty);
 return std::string(text);
}

// Extract integer from an element
std::expected<int, std::error_code>
get_element_int(const XmlElement* element) {
 int value = 0;
 if (!element->query_int_text(&value))
 return std::unexpected(xml_errc::parse_error);
 return value;
}

// Compose them with error handling
template <class T>
auto get_element_value(XmlElement* parent, std::string_view name) {
 if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int>) {
 return get_child_element(parent, name)
 .or_else(log_parse_error(name))
 .and_then(get_element_int);
 } else {
 return get_child_element(parent, name)
 .or_else(log_parse_error(name))
 .and_then(get_element_text);
 }
}

// Usage - clean and error-safe
auto name = get_element_value<std::string>(root, "username");
auto age = get_element_value<int>(root, "age");

if (name && age) {
 process_user(name.value(), age.value());
} else {
 // Errors already logged via or_else
 return std::unexpected(xml_errc::invalid_user_data);
}

This is similar to Rust’s ? operator or functional programming’s monadic composition. Each step automatically propagates errors, and .or_else() lets you handle errors inline without breaking the chain. No nested if-statements, no manual error propagation—the type system handles it.

Lessons learned

After working with both std::error_code and std::expected in production code, here are the key takeaways:

Do:

  • Use std::expected<T, std::error_code> for new APIs—it’s self-documenting and safe
  • Create custom error categories for domain-specific errors
  • Map custom errors to standard conditions via default_error_condition()
  • Leverage functional composition with .and_then(), .transform(), and .or_else()

Don’t:

  • Mix error handling styles in the same API boundary (exceptions + error codes + expected)
  • Forget that result.value() throws if the expected contains an error—use has_value() first or use value_or()
  • Create too many error categories—group related errors under one category

Performance notes:

  • Both std::error_code and std::expected are zero-cost abstractions
  • std::expected uses a tagged union internally—no heap allocations
  • Error message strings are only generated when you call .message(), not on construction

Migration path: If you’re converting an existing codebase:

  1. Start by wrapping std::error_code in std::expected at API boundaries
  2. Gradually convert internal functions to return std::expected directly
  3. Keep error categories consistent across old and new code

A gotcha: one error category object per program

This is important and non-obvious: an error category must be a single object for the whole program. If each translation unit ends up with its own copy, error comparisons break.

Why? The standard library’s error_category equality comparison uses pointer identity, not value comparison:

// Inside std::error_category
bool operator==(const error_category& rhs) const noexcept {
 return this == &rhs; // Pointer comparison!
}

If every translation unit has its own category object, the pointers differ, so comparisons fail, even though the objects represent the same category. That happens when the object has internal linkage, for example a static or anonymous-namespace instance defined in a header: each .cpp file that includes the header gets its own copy.

Being header-only is not the problem by itself. An inline function with a function-local static, or a C++17 inline variable, has one definition program-wide, so a category defined that way in a header is fine.

The safest fix: define the category instance in one .cpp file and hand it out by reference:

// http_response_code.cpp - NOT in the header!
namespace network {
 class http_error_category_impl final : public std::error_category { /* ... */ };

 const std::error_category& http_error_category() noexcept {
 static http_error_category_impl instance; // Single instance
 return instance;
 }
}

Note that the class and the function need different names. If both are called http_error_category, the function hides the class in that namespace and static http_error_category instance; does not compile.

Then in your header, only declare the function:

// http_response_code.h
namespace network {
 const std::error_category& http_error_category() noexcept;
}

If you do want a header-only category, define the class in the header and make the accessor inline:

// http_response_code.h
namespace network {
 class http_error_category_impl final : public std::error_category { /* ... */ };

 inline const std::error_category& http_error_category() noexcept {
 static http_error_category_impl instance;
 return instance;
 }
}

This gives every translation unit the same category instance, so the pointer comparisons work. One caveat remains across shared-library boundaries: if the header is compiled into two shared libraries (for example with hidden symbol visibility, or when you link it statically into two DSOs), each library can still end up with its own instance. Defining the category in one .cpp file in one library avoids that.

Conclusion

The combination of std::expected and std::error_code gives you the best of both worlds: type-safe APIs with rich, standardized error information. std::error_condition adds semantic weight by letting you classify errors generically (like HTTP’s client vs server errors) without checking individual codes.

It’s the current C++ way to handle errors without exceptions—just make sure each error category is a single object per program.

item.title: Typed Python CLI arguments with argparse and StrEnum
item.description:
Creating tools with python is a common practice due to its ease of use and productivity. Python already has good built-in support for parsing command-line arguments, but we can take it one step further.

Let’s take the following example where we would like to create a platform independent build script that should be able to accept the build type and an option to rebuild.

Since python3 we want to utilize the typing system as much as possible, meaning that the options the user can use as input for the commandline arguments are created from types so that if the types change the script arguments are automatically updated.

The ArgumentParser type parameter accepts a function that can help us to validate and transform the input data. A very useful class is StrEnum which, when inherited from, enables bidirectional conversion of string to enum. We can use this class to strictly declare which values our build_type argument accepts.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
r"""
Platform independent build script.
"""

import argparse
import errno
import os
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Final

try:
 from enum import StrEnum
except:
 raise Exception("Install python >= 3.11")


DEFAULT_SOLUTION_PATH: Final[Path] = Path("application.sln")


class BuildType(StrEnum):
 Debug = "Debug"
 Release = "Release"


def to_build_type(arg: str) -> BuildType:
 try:
 return BuildType[arg]
 except:
 raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"Invalid argument build_type '{arg}'")


def to_path(arg: str) -> Path:
 path = Path(arg)
 if path.exists():
 return path
 else:
 raise FileNotFoundError(errno.ENOENT, os.strerror(errno.ENOENT), arg)


def main(solution_path: Path, build_type: BuildType, rebuild: bool):
 print(
 f"{str(solution_path)} build_type={build_type} {'rebuild' if rebuild else ''}"
